source_read: PMC HTML (PMC7669776), full text read in my own browser tab on 2026-11-01: abstract, introduction, methods, results, Tables 1-4 (Table 1 recounted; every odds ratio in Tables 2-3 recomputed from the printed counts), discussion, conclusion, key points, references; Figures 1-2 not needed. To check the claim's mention of a correction, the publisher's article page (doi:10.1007/s12024-020-00291-8) was opened once in the same tab: version of record 22 August 2020, no change history or correction notice; the PMC record shows none either.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source; the claim is appropriately more cautious than the authors, who call their univariate comparisons of published case reports strong evidence and say restraint asphyxia must be considered a likely cause. Wording points: 'clinical reports describe survivors' should be 'clinical reports include survivors as well as deaths and use both labels' (Introduction, 5th paragraph); 'used mostly by forensic pathologists, and also by emergency physicians and others' is an inference from data sources (forensic-pathology literature almost exclusively uses the label; 10 of the 15 grouped ExDS studies used post-mortem sources), not a count of who applied the label in the case reports.
claims.note: Part not supported by this source: 'the authors later corrected one table'. No correction, erratum or change history appears on the PMC record or the publisher's page as of 2026-11-01; if a correction notice exists, cite it directly. What the tables do show: misassigned odds ratios in Table 2 (race; type of authority, repeated in the text) and Table 3 (race), and 100% mortality for Baldwin 2016 in Table 4 although its title describes non-fatal encounters. All claim and magnitude numbers check: 104/168 = 61.9%; 92/120 = 76.7% vs 12/48 = 25.0%, OR (92x36)/(28x12) = 9.86; some force in 94/104 deaths (90.4%; 2 none, 8 unknown) and 43/64 survivors (67.2%; Results text says 68%); no force 3 of 168, 2 fatal; cocaine 55/104 (52.9%) vs 19/64 (29.7%); police first 95/120 (79.2%) vs 16/48 (33.3%); 30 cases before 2000 (recounted from Table 1), 138 in 2000-2020, 90% and 56% fatal = 27 + 77 = 104. Drugs were coded from the most commonly described toxicities in each report, not from standardized toxicology. Minor slips: the Discussion gives individual-case ExDS mortality as 62%, which is the overall fatal share (ExDS alone 76.7%); Results 3rd paragraph prints n = 147 (86.3%) with drug intoxication and n = 138 (81.5%) with force, whose percentages fit 145 and 137, the counts Table 2 implies.

anchors.extracted: Neither ExDS nor AgDS is listed in ICD-9, ICD-10 or DSM-5; case descriptions and definitions are therefore unsystematic and nearly all research consists of retrospective case reports and series.

No autopsy findings indicate ExDS and intoxicant levels are typically recreational rather than fatally toxic (refs 6-7), so it is a diagnosis of exclusion; typical case: a man in his thirties, agitated and delirious, with drug use or mental illness, recent stimulant use, restrained at death, mostly by law enforcement. Wetli & Fishbain's 1985 series: 7 deaths, non-lethal blood cocaine (average 0.6 mg/L), no anatomical cause. A hypothesised cardiac calcium-channel mechanism has no supporting evidence.

ExDS is controversial as a cause of death when restraint occurred: agitation and delirium trigger forceful restraint, asphyxia leaves no specific autopsy signs, and risk factors for fatal ExDS (obesity, stimulant use, comorbidity) overlap completely with those for restraint asphyxia; some authors call the label a cover-up for excessive force. Forensic-pathology literature almost exclusively uses ExDS (all cases fatal); clinical literature uses ExDS and AgDS for the same presentation and includes non-fatal as well as fatal cases.

PubMed cross-referenced with Ovid Medline (445 hits) plus the top 1000 Google Scholar results, to 23 April 2020; 1342 screened; English-language case reports and series only, reviews excluded; diagnosis coded from the article's own term; use of force coded none, unknown, manhandle, handcuff, hog/hobble tie, TASER, sedation, other; drug intoxication from the most commonly described toxicities (none, unknown, cocaine, alcohol, marijuana, stimulants, other), categories not mutually exclusive; univariate chi-square or Fisher tests only.

1342 screened, 81 fully reviewed: 61 articles with individual cases (168 cases; one duplicate case omitted) and 20 grouped-data articles; men 161 (95.8%); law enforcement first on scene in 111 (66.1%); race missing in 95 (56.6%).

anchors.locator: Results › Analysis of outcome, 1st paragraph; Table 2
anchors.extracted: 104 of 168 (61.9%) died. ExDS in 92 of 104 deaths vs 28 of 64 survivors (OR 9.9). Cocaine noted 55 (52.9%) vs 19 (29.7%), OR 2.7; drug none noted 18 vs 3 (OR 4.3); marijuana 5 vs 21 (OR 0.1). Use of force none 2 vs 1, unknown 8 vs 20 (OR 0.18); manhandle 68 vs 13 (OR 7.4), handcuff 74 vs 12 (OR 10.7), hog/hobble tie 46 vs 1 (OR 50), sedation 6 vs 40 (OR 0.04). Police first on scene 87 vs 24.

anchors.locator: Results › Analysis of diagnosis, 1st paragraph; Table 3
anchors.extracted: ExDS 120 (71.4%), AgDS 48 (28.6%); died 92/120 (76.7%) vs 12/48 (25.0%), OR 9.9; police first on scene 95 (79.2%) vs 16 (33.3%); manhandle OR 4.7, handcuff 14, hog/hobble tie 29.2; sedation 16 vs 30 (OR 0.09); cocaine 60 vs 14 (OR 2.4).

Some restraint described in 90% of deaths (2 deaths with none, 8 unknown or missing) vs 67% of survivors (43; 1 none, 20 unknown); authors infer that ExDS is not a unique cause of death without restraint, granting it is possible but finding no observational evidence for death without restraint.

Vilke et al. (2012 review) gave ExDS fatality as under 10% and the 2009 ACEP white paper (DeBard et al.) as 8.3%; both cite Barnett et al. 2007, a first-episode psychosis paper with no mortality figures, in which 8.3 is the SD of IQ. The white paper called ExDS a unique clinical entity and recommended the term for emergency medicine; Strömmer notes shared authorship with experimental restraint studies in healthy volunteers.

Fatal share 90% of the 30 cases published before 2000 and 56% of the 138 published 2000-2020; the authors attribute the fall to awareness of restraint asphyxia and do not consider a change in the mix of clinical and forensic reports.

anchors.locator: Results › Analysis of group data studies, 1st paragraph; Table 4
anchors.extracted: 19 grouped studies (one overlapping pair merged): 4 AgDS studies, 153 cases, 5 deaths (3%); 15 ExDS studies, 666 cases, 529 deaths (79%); 10 post-mortem, 7 hospital and 2 police data sources; the 7 low- or zero-mortality studies were hospital-based or police-based, including 3 of the 4 AgDS studies; only 8 of 19 described restraint. Table 4 gives 100% mortality for Baldwin 2016 (73 cases), titled as non-fatal use-of-force encounters; at 0% the ExDS total would be 456 of 666 (68%).

Cocaine associated with 2.7-fold odds of death, marijuana and other drugs with survival; the authors explain this through restraint (stimulants provoke combative behaviour and forceful restraint, sedating drugs less so; Fig. 2), an untested interpretation. They argue from US 2010 consumption and death estimates that the per-use risk of death from methamphetamine is at most about 1 in 353,000, so drug presence should not be preferred over restraint as the cause.

Limitations: the labels have no ICD codes, so cases cannot be found in hospital databases; fatal cases are over-represented and better documented (toxicology, police reports, witnesses); not a random sample; reports often lack which drugs, amounts, tolerance and whether a drug was judged an overdose or contributory; restraint type, duration and force often missing.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 9th and 12th paragraphs; Conclusion; Key points 3-4
anchors.extracted: The literature's limits cut both ways. Proposals: abandon ExDS for agitated delirium with a restraint modifier (none, mild, aggressive); manner of death for fatal AgDS after restraint homicide or undetermined, not natural or accident; full autopsy with toxicology and a review of restraint. For the 2 deaths without described restraint, psychosis or intoxication may have caused an arrhythmia, but no reliable conclusion is possible.
